newsitem.title: USA: Democrats -- odds even on U.S. budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: Democrats -- odds even on U.S. budget amendment.

text.p: Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle said Monday chances of Senate approval of the balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution were at best fifty-fifty with the momentum against the amendment.

"I don't believe that the constitutional amendment is in as strong a position as it was a week ago," the South Dakota Democrat said at his regular news conference. At best their prospects for passage are fifty-fifty," he said. Another Democrat announced his opposition last Thursday.
Democrats are one vote shy of enough to defeat the amendment with two of their colleagues still undecided.

Two Democrats, Sens. Mary Landrieu of Louisiana and Robert Toricelli of New Jersey, pledged during their campaigns to vote for a constitutional balanced budget amendment but have not said if they will vote for the Republican version before the Senate.

The Senate faces critical votes this week on Democratic proposals to exempt Social Security from the balanced budget calculation, a move they argued will protect retirement benefits in the next century. A final vote on the amendment was still expected this week although on Sunday an influential Republican lawmaker recommended it be delayed.
House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, Republican of Ohio, said he doubted Senate Republicans had the votes now to pass the amendment.

Sen. Harry Reid, D-Nevada, sponsor of the Social Security exemption proposal, accused Republicans of using the balanced budget amendment as a way to cut the program. "It will enshrine in the constitution stealing all these monies," he said at the news conference with Daschle.

Under the balanced budget amendment, the government would be required to balance each year's spending with revenues expected for that same year. Democrats charge this would bar the government from using Social Security surpluses to meet retirement claims in the the next century when the annual payroll taxes will be smaller than benefits owed.

For several years Congress and the White House have debated whether Social Security funds should have a budget separate from the rest of government. Currently, the government borrows from the Social Security system to pay its annual bills.
While taking Social Security off the budget would make it more difficult to balance the budget, Daschle said this could be phased in as the government moves to balance the budget.
